sections.report:
Walk (working notes):

First read: the eye lands on the large title "Planning a vegetable bed" at top left, then moves down the three headings (soil, what to plant, watering). It reads as a short how-to for a beginner gardener. It feels calm and plain, close to a bare document. Assumed job: a short beginner's guide on a web page that tells you how to set up a first vegetable bed.

The whole piece:
- One-sentence purpose: yes
- Main image and headline make one idea: yes (no image, so nothing to fail)
- Every element does a job: yes
- One mood and era: yes
- Copy finished, no placeholders or typos: yes
- Repeated elements look the same: yes (the three section headings match)
- Colors, shapes and directions fit the mood: yes (plain black on white suits a calm, practical how-to)
- Each heading names its section: yes

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so step 5 is not needed.

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- The copy is concrete and complete. Each paragraph tells the reader one action with a real measure ("six hours of sun", "the depth of a spade", "twice a week"), so a beginner can act without guessing. The words are the strongest part of the piece.
- Nothing is extra. There are no rules, boxes, icons or colour, and the four blocks use one repeated heading-and-paragraph pattern. You can see the page's purpose and structure at once.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

I found one minor issue in the hierarchy section. Bash was blocked, so I couldn't run the crop script. I worked from the whole image, which is about one screen (around 1280×800), and opened the reference entry with the Read tool instead.

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **The headings don't differ from the text in weight, form, or color as well as size.** This affects "Preparing the soil", "Choosing what to plant", and "Watering" (x≈160, y≈225, 352 and 478). They look like the same regular weight, upright style and near-black as the body text below them. The only difference is size, about 32 px against about 18 px.
   - **What the viewer sees:** the headings are easy to find because the size jump is large, so nothing is lost. But the page reads as a plain size ramp. The headings look like enlarged body text rather than markers set apart from the copy. The title is in the same light weight, so all four levels feel like one voice getting louder.
   - **Source:** Dair, *Design with Type*, chapters 8a to 8g and 9. Plain work builds every level from size alone. Better work pairs a smaller size step with a second contrast.
   - **Fix:** give the headings a heavier weight (medium or semibold) or a distinct color, and then shrink them a step, to about 22–24 px. The size jump can be smaller when weight does part of the work. The page also gets tighter and more even.
   - **Type and weight:** convention, minor. This is the mild end of the defect: the size step is clear, so the order still reads correctly.

**What's working.**
- **A clear starting point.** The title, at about 52 px, is far larger than anything else, so the eye has no doubt where to start (layout.md "One element dominates").
- **A tight type scale.** There are three sizes in big steps (≈52, ≈32 and ≈18 px), with no near-duplicates. The intro paragraph is rightly set as body text, not as a fourth size.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (headings differ from the text in more than size)

sections.report:
**Walk: Arrangement and space** (no crops needed: the image is about 1280×800, one screen. Bash is not permitted here, so I worked from the whole image.)

First read: the eye lands on the title "Planning a vegetable bed" (top left, about 160–733 px wide, y≈60–112). It then moves down a single left-aligned stack: an intro paragraph and three headed sections. It reads as a short how-to article or help page, calm and plain. Assumed job: a web article that a home gardener reads from top to bottom.

1. One grid: yes. There is one column and every block starts at x≈160.
2. Exact alignment, no near-misses: yes. The title, intro, headings and body all share the x≈160 edge.
3. Baselines across columns: yes. There is only one column.
4. Space inside groups smaller than between groups: yes. Each heading sits about 10–15 px above its body (for example "Preparing the soil" at y≈228–258, with the body starting at y≈272). The gap between sections is about 30–35 px (body ends at y≈320, next heading starts at y≈352). The intro sits about the same distance from the title as from the first heading, but it is above a heading, so it cannot be read as part of that section.
5. Boxes holding one group: yes. There are no boxes.
6. No accidental groups: yes.
7. No overlap or touching: yes.
8. Margin from the edge: yes. About 160 px on the left and about 60 px at the top.
9. Empty space gathered: yes. It falls in one band on the right (x≈950–1280) and one at the bottom (y≈550–800).
10. Balance: yes. The weight sits top-left, which is normal for a left-aligned reading column, and the page does not look like it is tipping.
11. Centering by habit: yes. Nothing is centered.
12. Proportional divisions: yes. The column is about 800 of 1280 px (about 0.62), and the left margin is about 1/8 of the width.
13. Eye path: yes. The eye moves straight from top to bottom and nothing leads it off the page.

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so there were no entries to open.

---

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **Spacing makes the groups clear.** Each heading sits about 10–15 px above its own paragraph and about 30–35 px below the previous one (for example "Choosing what to plant" at y≈352, after body text ending at y≈320). This makes three clear units you can scan without rules or boxes. Keep the gap between sections at least about twice the gap between heading and body.
- **One left edge.** The title, intro, headings and body all hang from x≈160 with no near-misses. That gives the page a single strong edge for the eye to follow down. Keep it if you add elements such as pictures or callouts.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the column stays left-anchored or re-centers at other widths. At 1280 px it leaves about 330 px empty on the right, which is fine as long as the page reflows sensibly on narrower and wider screens.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 13 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
The walk is done, so I'm writing the report now.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do paragraph lines run about 45 to 75 characters?** No. All four paragraphs fill a column about 790 px wide (x≈160–950), so the full lines run about 85–92 characters. Examples are "Dig to the depth of a spade and mix in compost from last year's heap. Rake the surface level" (y≈281) and "Choose a spot that gets six hours of sun and stays out of the wind. Mark the corners with" (y≈155). On every return sweep the reader has a long way back to the start of the next line, which makes it easier to lose your place and makes the page read a little slower than this easy text should. The generous line spacing (about 28 px on about 17 px text) helps, which is why the cost stays small. Bringhurst gives 45–75 characters, with 66 as the ideal (*Elements*, 2.1.2, p. 26). Fix: narrow the text column to about 600–640 px at this size, or raise the body size a step. The right half of the canvas is already empty, so this costs nothing. Convention. Weight: minor, because the paragraphs are only two lines each.
2. **Are large headings set with tighter letter and word spacing than the text?** No. The title "Planning a vegetable bed" (x 160–733, y≈60–115, about 56 px, light weight) looks like it is set with the face's default text spacing. At this size its letter and word gaps look slightly open, so the title feels airy and loosely assembled rather than like one solid line. Lupton notes that letter spacing grows with size and needs adjusting in large type (*Thinking with Type*, p. 80). Bringhurst says word spacing can tighten as well at larger sizes (2.1.1, p. 26). Fix: apply a small negative tracking (around -1% to -2%) to the title, or use the family's display cut if it has one. Don't overdo it, since Lupton warns that negative tracking should be used sparingly. Convention. Weight: minor.
3. **Are quotation marks curly, and are dashes and ellipses the true characters?** No. The apostrophe in "last year's" (about x 640, y 281) is a straight typewriter mark, not a typographic apostrophe. At 17 px almost no reader will notice it, but it shows the copy went in without smart punctuation, and the same mark will stand out in any larger heading or pull quote later. Fix: switch on smart quotes in the content pipeline, or type ’. Taste and common sense: the catalog entry says no checked source covers curly versus straight quotes. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- Body text is a plain, upright sans at a comfortable size (about 17 px), near-black on white, with generous line spacing (about 1.65). It is easy to read, and the long measure costs less than it otherwise would.
- The text is clean: a single family, flush-left paragraphs, a soft rag with no runts, and four short chunks under plain headings. A gardener can skim straight to "Watering".

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 27 yes, 3 no (lines of 45 to 75 characters; large headings spaced tighter; curly quotes and true dashes)

**Walk (working notes)**

Crop script and Bash are refused, so I'm working from the whole image (about 1280×800, one screen).

First read: the eye lands on the large title "Planning a vegetable bed" (top left, about y 60–115). It then moves down the three subheads. This looks like a short how-to article or help page for beginner gardeners, and it feels calm, plain and unbranded. There is no colour at all: near-black text, possibly a dark blue-gray, on a white page.

Job, assumed: a short instructional article for home gardeners, to be read on screen.

Color:
- Small palette: yes. One neutral range only.
- Strong colour kept to a small share of the area: yes. There is no saturated colour.
- Clear range of light and dark: yes. Dark text on white has full value contrast and keeps its structure in grayscale.
- Warm forward, cool back: yes. There are no hues to misplace.
- Matching colours look the same: yes. Title, subheads and body all look like the same dark ink.
- Neighbouring strong colours differ in lightness: yes. There are none.
- Status colours used only for their usual meaning: yes. There are none.
- Meaning shown by colour is also shown another way: yes. Nothing relies on colour.
- Dark theme uses dark gray: yes. This is a light theme, so the line doesn't apply.

No line came out `no` or `unsure`, so step 5 had no entries to open.

---

**Section.** Color: applies. The piece is fully achromatic: dark text on white.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** 
- **Value does all the work.** One dark ink on white gives the full light-to-dark range. The body text is easy to read, and the structure (title, subheads, paragraphs) holds in grayscale because colour plays no part in it. Keep this if colour is added later: put any new hue on top of this value structure, not in its place.
- **The ink is a soft near-black, not pure #000.** The headings and body look like a slightly softened dark tone. That makes the page less harsh on white without costing contrast (Refactoring UI's advice to avoid pure black). Check the exact value in a live browser to confirm.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure
